A young myrmidon of the Colosso who has filled out into a fighter, Hadrian's friend since his first days in the pit. He forgives Hadrian and agrees to be his second in the duel against Gilliam Vas.

summary.text: A foederati mercenary company under Sir Alexei Karelin, attached to the Legions.
A rival foederati company under Arno Cousland, which Kogan sneers at as paper-pushers and parade marchers.
The alien species at war with humanity, the pale monsters who raze cities, burn planets and carry off people to be slaves or meat.

The alien enemy of the Empire, a nomadic, carnivorous species that lives in migratory clusters called scianda. Hadrian argues they cannot be exterminated, because a single escaping ship is enough for them to survive.
The alien enemy of humanity, nomadic and carnivorous. Hadrian speaks their language almost fluently, which makes the Chantry devout suspicious of him.

The alien enemy of humanity, pale, white-skinned beings with horned crests, glassy claws and four slit nostrils, who call themselves the People. A crashed Cielcin crew has been met face to face on Emesh, and Hadrian is the only man who can speak with them.
Humanity's lost homeworld, from which the ancestors set out in their leaking ships; the Chantry and the faithful still revere it.
An order of learned men and women, tutors with trained memories, who do the work forbidden thinking machines would do. Gibson is one.

An ancient order of philosopher-priests who counsel Emperors and sail to strange planets, trained to remember everything and forbidden to use machines, tracing their founding to the days of the machine-lords.

An ancient order of scholars with minds trained to perfect memory, said to have been founded by the few Mericanii who survived the Foundation War. They carry a stigma, and the Chantry's devout look on them with suspicion.
The title scholiasts bear before their names, as in Tor Gibson.
The prefecture of Delos that Alistair Marlowe governs as Archon, and the city beneath the castle of Devil’s Rest.
The prefecture of Delos governed by Alistair Marlowe, and its city beneath the limestone cliffs below the castle of Devil’s Rest.
The Marlowe castle above Meidua, a palace of dark stone where Hadrian grew up.
The Marlowe castle on the cliffs above Meidua, a black fortress with a great keep, a Chantry sanctum and a throne room, guarded by peltasts and hoplites. It is the seat of the Lord of Devil’s Rest.
The planet where Hadrian was born, of which his grandmother the vicereine is duchess.
Hadrian's homeworld, a planet far from the war front, with a vast grey ocean beyond the castle's curtain wall; the Marlowes' uranium has made them its richest family.
The place that gives Hadrian's father his nickname, the Butcher of Linon.
An airless world half a system from Meidua where House Orin's castle now lies in ruins; Alistair destroyed House Orin there when it rebelled.
A noble house of Linon that rebelled against Alistair Marlowe.
A noble house of Linon whose lord refused the Archon his tribute and raised an army against him. Alistair destroyed it, and its castle is a shattered ruin.
The place where the war with the Cielcin is fought, where the Veil opens on the Norma Arm, some twenty thousand light-years from Delos.
The frontier where the war with the Cielcin is fought, beyond the Centaurus Arm, where colonies are harried by the Cielcin.
The spiral arm of the galaxy out where the Veil opens, the far front of the war against the Cielcin.
The place of the first battle between the Empire and the Cielcin, some three hundred years before Hadrian's birth.
The Empire's long war against the Cielcin, already three hundred years old when Hadrian was born.
An archive world where billions of manuscripts lie, and where Hadrian says he has left his own account.
The Empire's armies, which levy conscripts from the plebeians every decade.

The Empire's armies, which levy conscripts from the plebeians every decade. A recruitment advertisement shows a woman in the bone-coloured armour of the Imperial Legions, and the Legions fight the Cielcin along the frontier.
An interstellar trading combine, through which the Marlowes sell their uranium.
One of the great institutions that bind the human universe together, with Yamato Interstellar, the Rothsbank and the Free Traders Union. Its Mandari delegation comes to Delos to buy uranium.
An interstellar trading institution, through which the Marlowes sell their uranium.
A trading institution whose independent ship captains, Free Traders, carry cargo and passengers between the stars, outside the Empire's regular lines and rather like pirates.
One of the great institutions that bind the human universe together.
One of the great interstellar institutions, a bank, with which one can hold an account or take out a loan.
The guild of miners on Delos, whose representatives like Lena Balem press the Archon for new equipment.
A great noble who governs a province of the Empire for the Emperor; Hadrian's grandmother is one.
The Empire's church, the Holy Terran Chantry, whose priests are chanters and priors. Its holiest law forbids the thinking machines called daimons.
The Empire's church, which controls the use and trade of all complex machinery. It hunts daimons and maintains the Inquisition.
The Empire's church, an instrument of terror and awe that regulates what people may do and punishes offenders. It trains its inquisitors at seminaries such as Lorica College on Vesperad.

The Empire's church, which holds Emesh through its grand prior and its bastille. Its inquisitor and cathars torture captured Cielcin, and its Twelve Abominations include the perversion of the body with machines.
The Chantry's torturers and executioners, silent men in black who carry out its punishments.
Blindfolded, black-robed torturers of the Chantry, with porcelain skin, who scourge, mutilate and kill at its orders.

Silent, bald, black-robed torturers of the Chantry, blindfolded and porcelain-skinned. In the bastille at Borosevo they torture the captive Cielcin with a lead-spraying mace, and one of them is killed.
The Chantry's punitive body, which tortures and sterilizes planets that break its rules.
The Chantry's punitive body, whose inquisitors advise the Legions and are said to drop atomic weapons on the Pale.
The Chantry's punitive body, whose Holy Office examines the conduct of nobles and is invoked to punish them.
The thinking machines that the Chantry's holiest law forbids; scholiasts train their minds to do what such machines would do.

The intelligent machines with which the Mericanii once oppressed the rest of humankind, and which in turn oppressed them. The Chantry controls complex machinery to hunt for them, though none has appeared in Imperial space for two thousand years.
The ancient machine-lords who ruled sixteen thousand years ago, linked to the founding of the Empire.
The ancient machine-lords, dead sixteen thousand years, who oppressed humankind with their intelligent machines and were oppressed by them in turn.
The ancient machine-lords of the distant past. A few of them survived the Foundation War and founded the order of the scholiasts.
An ancient war which the few Mericanii who survived it did not forget; the scholiasts trace their order to them.
The Empire's highest nobility, bred to be tall, strong and long-lived, who wear signet rings and fight by their own code.
The Empire's highest nobility. A palatine's signet ring holds his identity, genetic history, titles and the deeds to his holdings, and palatine houses honour the rules of poine when a man yields.
A commoner, whose blood the High College has not doctored; plebeians age quickly and are levied for the Legions.
A grade of the Empire's population above the plebeians, with some enhancements to their genes; Sir Roban is one.
A noble person, a member of the great houses; marriages among nobiles are often political necessities.
The institution that watches over the births of nobles, making sure their genetic deviations have not turned to defects.
The institution that oversees the genetic stock of the nobility. Plebeians like Lena Balem go untreated by it.
A shield technology that deflects bullets and plasma bursts but not swords.
The material of the finest swords; a highmatter blade can cut through almost anything, which is why a fighter must not rest one on his shoulder.
The human empire of the Emperors on the Solar Throne, ruled by palatine lords and vicereines, which is at war with the Cielcin.
The Emperor of the House Avent, in whose name the herald announces the Archon.
The imperial house to which the Emperor belongs.
The Emperor's seat of power, said to stand on Forum, built to make the Emperor loom over every supplicant.
The seat of the Emperor's throne, the heart of the Empire.
A far-flung realm whose people are known for fire-poetry and swordmasters; its satraps and princes are not Imperial lords.
A far-off realm where satraps and princes bend to the demands of industry; its people speak the Jaddian language and fight with famed swordmasters.
A realm of princes that rebelled long ago from the Empire's Forum and won independence, known for breeding its palatines for beauty, for cloned mamluk soldiers and for its swordmasters.
The swordmasters of Jadd, who perform menial tasks for years before they are allowed to touch a sword.
The famed swordmasters of Jadd, who are trained from youth. Hadrian is told he is no Maeskolos.
A trade language of the Consortium, spoken by the Mandari and by interstellar corporations.
The people of the merchant stations and trading houses of the Consortium, who speak Mandar; the visitors to Delos are Mandari.
A guttural language without personal pronouns or names, used by Hadrian and Gibson for secrecy, and the people who speak it.
One of the Empire's languages, spoken by Hadrian and by many nobles and priests.
An ancient tongue that scholiasts quote and Chantry rites are spoken in.
A planet destroyed by the Cielcin, with millions of lives lost.
The entangled-particle telegraph that carries messages between the stars.
The corps that travels the stars on exploration; Hadrian dreams of joining it.
Barbarians who live between the stars, preying on trading vessels, in black-masted ships.
The barbarians who ply the Dark in black-masted ships and prey on trading vessels. In legend they burned a city of poets, and their kings are called the Exalted.

The barbarians who ply the Dark in black-masted ships, whom Hadrian pictures as barely human shapes that gave themselves to daimon machines. A dying Cielcin captain's words suggest that the Cielcin have met humans between the stars, which Hadrian takes to mean them.
The space between the stars.
The Cielcin word for one of their migratory clusters of ships.
A high rank of the Orionid Legions.
The noble house of Hadrian's mother and her mother the vicereine, whose emblem is an eagle.
The people of Tavros, a polity at the edge of the galaxy outside the Chantry's control, with languages of their own.
The people of the Tavros Demarchy, a polity beyond the Chantry's reach; the Chantry would let Hadrian see it as an inquisitor.

A group of clans at the edge of the galaxy with a culture distinct from the Empire's. Their languages include Nordei, Panthai and Travatsk, and their Demarchy gives every adult a weighted share of the vote.
A Chantry officer who hunts heretics and advises the Legions.
The noble house of Hadrian and his father, which has become the largest licensed supplier of uranium.
The metal the Marlowe lands produce, shipped as yellow cake downriver, the source of their wealth.
The rotunda and council chamber of Devil’s Rest, filled with ancient statues and stained glass.
The massive square-sided bastion of steel and dark stone at the centre of Devil’s Rest, where Hadrian has his rooms.
A political entity beyond the Empire, whose Lothrian language Hadrian studies; Ascia is among its worlds.
The Empire's administration, from which a baron's title might be bought.
A summer palace in the hill country where Hadrian's mother retreats.
The summer palace of the vicereine in the hill country, seven hectares of retreat where Hadrian's mother keeps her household and where he waits to be sent to Vesperad.
A place on Delos where the vicereine and Hadrian's father are absent on state business; the ducal palace there is larger than Devil’s Rest.
The Empire's great spectacle of beast-baiting and slave melees staged in a coliseum.
The Empire's great spectacle of beast-baiting and gladiatorial fights. At Borosevo the Colosso is run by the count and Lord Balian, and keeps a pool of desperate fighters called myrmidons.
The handlers of the Colosso who control beasts and slaves with stun rods.
Human overseers who guard and beat the Umandh slave workers on Emesh.
An offworld flying beast like a pterosaur crossed with a dragon, with a long neck and hooked teeth, baited in the coliseum.
A team of seven performers dressed as legionnaires, who fight slaves painted as Cielcin in the Meidua Colosso.
A colony where the 617th Centaurine Legion was stranded, used as the setting of a Colosso spectacle.
The manager of a Colosso, who decides the details of the fights; a similar title is used for the overseer of the Umandh island.
The rules by which palatine houses grant surrender and ransom when a man yields.
A palatine's ring, holding his identity, genetic history, titles and the deeds to his holdings.
Freedom from emotion, sought by scholiasts.
A list Gibson makes Hadrian recite, of the kinds of obedience, from fear of pain to devotion.
A scholiast's list of eight kinds of obedience, beginning with obedience out of fear of pain, which Gibson calls the law of the fishes, and ending with obedience out of piety.
The world where the Chantry's seminary Lorica College stands, to which Hadrian's father orders him.
The world where the Chantry's Synod meets, the greatest seat of holy authority, and where the seminary of Lorica College stands.
The Chantry seminary on Vesperad where Hadrian is ordered to train as an inquisitor.
A high-ranking body of the Chantry.
The long spread of humanity among the stars, which Crispin says Earth died to inspire.
The interstellar province of four hundred stars that Hadrian's grandmother governs as vicereine.
A month of the Delian calendar, marking the start of autumn.
Nomad caravaners with a net of asteroid stations, also players of masques and melodrama; Hadrian's speech is said to sound like a villain in a Eudoran opera.
The inbred colonies of the Normans, held up by Hadrian's father as an example of disorder.
Hadrian's name for the devotion to Earth, with its icona, that he considers false.
The sacred images of the Chantry, printed on cheap plastic in the streets or kept in the sanctum, of Death, Fortitude, Ever-Fleeting Time and others.
An artificial person bred and tailored for a task, such as a herald or a pet; regarded as not quite human.
The battle that helped Alistair make the lords forget the embarrassment of his rise to power.
A world with a scholiasts' athenaeum, where Hadrian plans to flee with Gibson's letter.
A scholiasts' college; Teukros has one.
The Empire's standard currency, available only to those with high-status occupations; a starship is priced in millions of marks.
Gold coins bearing the Emperor's profile, the money of the lower strata of society.
Silver coins of the street, with steel bits as small change; paper notes are worth a twelfth or five kaspums.
The trading cog on which Hadrian is officially to depart for Vesperad.
The title of the Mining Guild's representative.
A lower officer of the Chantry, below a chanter.
A massive, unpointed ceramic blade used by cathars for executions; Hadrian's father withheld it from Gibson.
A knife that glows star-hot and cauterizes as it cuts, used by the cathars.
The Earth as the faithful call it.
A world mentioned as a possible destination for the escape.
A port on Teukros where a merchant ship could take Hadrian.
The kingdom of the pirate Kharn Sagara.
A frigid world with a dead star, taken by Kharn Sagara for himself after he turned the Exalted against one another.
A world of legend that the dying Cielcin captain Uvanari named as the place where it had met humans, between the stars. Hadrian is startled, because he thought it a myth.

A pirate world of legend, the kingdom of Kharn Sagara. The count calls it nonsense, but Lady Kalima argues it may be real, and Hadrian argues that the Cielcin captain's naming of it points to an Extrasolarian world out there.
An island city in the Apollan Ocean on Delos, where Hadrian is to meet his contact.
The vast grey ocean beyond Devil’s Rest.
The Jaddian ship of the Free Trader Demetri, which carries Hadrian.
The Jaddian ship of the Free Trader Demetri, with fugue crèches in its medica. Its journey to Teukros was to take thirteen years in fugue.
A stopover on the route to Teukros.
A world on the route to Teukros, two years beyond Obatala.
An avian species of flying xenobites who ruled a freezing, craggy world and serve as auxilia in the Legions.
The race of flying xenobites on Judecca, whose princes Simeon the Red befriended; the Irchtani now fight as auxilia in the Imperial Legions against the Cielcin.
The planet that Simeon the Red named for the treason suffered there, home of the Irchtani; Hadrian dreams of sailing there.
The Eurynasir's helmsman's contemptuous word for scholiasts.
The Delian Defense Force, which Bassem fears will pursue the Eurynasir.
Hadrian's word for the frozen sleep of long space voyages, in which a traveller is carried across the stars for years.
A cryonic suspension chamber with a dark glass front, used for long journeys between stars.
The planet in the Veil where Hadrian wakes, with a red sun and green water, whose gravity is heavier than that of Delos.
A planet of storms and canals in the Veil, once colonised by the Norman United Fellowship before the Empire seized it, held by House Mataro.
The city where Hadrian lived among the poor as a myrmidon called Had.
A city on Emesh built on steel pilings at the water's edge, with a starport and a palace ziggurat, where Hadrian is stranded.
A city of Emesh built on an atoll, home to five million, with urban farms, fisheries and warehouses.
A plague on Emesh caused by an alien animalcule that blackens the skin and wastes the flesh.
A sickness brought to Emesh by an offworld trader that chews through its natives, causing sores and rot; Hadrian's palatine blood protects him, but Cat dies of it.
The wealthy part of Borosevo built into a bulwark, home of patricians and guild members, with a copper-domed Chantry sanctum.
The warren of canals and low buildings below the White District, where the poor live.
The weekly day on which beggars are tolerated in the White District.
The police of Borosevo, who wear dun khakis and carry stunners.
A weapon that makes the muscles slack and the target helpless with pain.
A people of the frontier, builders of cheap and fast ships, who once held Emesh as the Norman United Fellowship until the Empire took it.
Emeshi street slang for an outsider or fellow.
A list of marvels that Hadrian wanted to see as a boy.
A client republic of the Empire with a heavy, guttural language, home of the medic Chand.
A seer or prophet; a naked, sun-crazed one preaches on a scaffold in Borosevo.
The weekly service of the Chantry, at which beggars are tolerated.
A place with woods of silver trees where Cat's mother said fairies lived; they were really insects drawn to the trees.
The sandstone castle atop a terraced concrete ziggurat that dominates Borosevo, the Count of Emesh's seat.
The holiest temple of the Irchtani on the highest mountain of Judecca, where Simeon the Red has his tomb.
The native species of Emesh: squat, three-legged beings with flesh like coral or stone. Humans enslave them as workers, and call them coloni.
The three-legged, scaly natives of Emesh, used as slaves. They talk in droning chords, and the doctor Valka thinks they work together like a combined organism.
The three-legged, scaly natives of Emesh, used as slaves. In the fish warehouse they went berserk and killed three people, among them the vilicus Engin, and Hadrian killed one with a machete.
The native races enslaved on their own worlds; on Emesh the word means the Umandh.
An extinct civilisation of Ozymandias, dead forty-three hundred years.
A government body that guarantees a base-level job to anyone on Emesh, but requires blood-typing and screening; it also sends thugs to reeducation.
The department of the Borosevo Prefects' Office that handles crime scenes.
The Emeshi thieves' word for the conditioning surgeons who straighten a criminal's head.
The title Hadrian says the poor of Borosevo knew him by, a gladiator.
The men and women of the Colosso's fodder pool, broken, mad, convict or desperate fighters, less than professional gladiators.
The Colosso's pool of desperate or convicted fighters, who serve as fodder for the professional gladiators.
A cold passage leading into the arena, separated from the heat outside by a static field.
The noble house of the planet Emesh, in whose dominion Hadrian wakes.
The noble house of Emesh, which co-owns the Colosso games with Lord Balian.
The team of five professional gladiators that fight the myrmidons.
The round three-foot carbon-fibre shield used by the myrmidons.
A Chantry icon, invoked in prayer.
A belt that projects a protective shield.
Contract soldiers or mercenaries serving with the Legions.
A palatine with genetic mutations or defects; a derogatory word for such a person.
The Legion Intelligence Office, which receives Cielcin hostages.
The site of a battle in which a Cielcin worldship fortress was destroyed and prisoners taken.
An Imperial ship that carried foederati and legionnaire dropouts to Emesh.
An Imperial carrier of the Legion in orbit above Borosevo, to which the Knight-Tribune orders the Cielcin captives delivered, and from which Hadrian's mission is to set out.
An old, durable make of freighter, built at the Andun shipyards.
A sleek crimson ship, shaped like an arrowhead, that Hadrian admires at the repo docks.
The county service of Emesh, which sells repossessed ships.
A captive Cielcin held in a cell below the Colosso, which Hadrian reaches by sneaking in past the guards.
A Cielcin held in a cell beneath the Colosso, who is to be sacrificed for the count's son's Ephebeia. Hadrian speaks to him in the Cielcin tongue and is stunned by a guard.
A Cielcin held in the count's gaol, which the chanter Gilliam Vas bought from the foederati for the coming sacrifice.
A Cielcin captive, drugged and led in chains in the Chantry triumph for Dorian's Ephebeia. A cathar beheaded him with the White Sword and presented his head to Dorian.

The author of a treatise called Unnatural Grammars, whose idea about language and civilisation Hadrian and Valka discuss.
A scholiast whose treatise Unnatural Grammars argues that language is needed for civilisation to develop.
A treatise by Philemon of Neruda on language and the growth of civilisation, which Hadrian and Valka argue over when she studies the Umandh.
The current master at arms of the count's children, hideous and not much of a teacher.
The author of Cyrus the Fool, a play performed by Eudoran players at the coliseum.
A play by Bastien about a prince who survives atmospheric re-entry, performed by Eudoran mummers at the coliseum.
Someone Hadrian, looking back, wonders about when he doubts whether the Empire's people are anything but barbarians.
A Tavrosi woman whom Hadrian knew by her tattoos, which tell a clansman's genetic and personal history in a symbolic language he could not read.
A slender, pale woman with an intricately tattooed arm who stops a douleter from beating an Umandh and introduces herself as Valka Onderra Vhad Edda, xenologist.
